definition: in a way that suggests a favorable outcome
memoryTip: Auspicious omens once came from watching birds — a promising start.
correctPassage: The festival began auspiciously with clear skies and a packed opening night.
wrongPassages: The merger opened auspiciously when both CEOs resigned on day one.
Rain flooded the field, so the season started auspiciously for outdoor sports.
She took the rejection letter as an auspiciously clear sign to quit altogether.

definition: in a random, unplanned, or careless way
memoryTip: Hap (chance) + hazard — by luck, not by plan; messy.
correctPassage: Files had been stored haphazardly, with no consistent naming system.
wrongPassages: The engineer arranged every cable haphazardly according to a detailed blueprint.
She packed haphazardly, labeling each box and checking items off a list.
They marched haphazardly in perfect formation down the parade route.

memoryTip: Like a story’s antagonist — opposing, not cooperative.
correctPassage: The two theories are not necessarily antagonistic; they address different scales.
wrongPassages: Her antagonistic tone put everyone at ease within the first minute.
The partners signed an antagonistic agreement to share profits equally.
Neighbors held an antagonistic block party to welcome new families.

definition: a summary; the act of adding things up
memoryTip: Sum it up — a total or a closing overview.
correctPassage: The final chapter is a careful summation of the book’s main claims.
wrongPassages: Her summation skipped any overview and opened with brand-new evidence.
He offered a summation that listed every footnote and never closed the argument.
The lawyer’s summation was a raw first draft she had not yet organized.

definition: leaving no doubt; clear and unambiguous
memoryTip: Un-equi-vocal: not two voices — one clear meaning only.
correctPassage: The data provide unequivocal support for the revised timeline.
wrongPassages: His unequivocal answer was “maybe, depending on several unknowns.”
The map was unequivocal: three conflicting routes and no legend.
She gave an unequivocal shrug that left the committee more confused than before.

memoryTip: You can’t reproach (blame) them — conduct with no fault to find.
correctPassage: Her professional conduct throughout the inquiry was irreproachable.
wrongPassages: The audit found his irreproachable books riddled with missing receipts.
Critics praised the film as irreproachable for its endless plot holes.
An irreproachable alibi collapsed when security video showed him at the scene.

definition: relating to mental links or connections between ideas
memoryTip: Works by association — memory links, not strict step-by-step logic.
correctPassage: The poem relies on associative leaps rather than a linear plot.
wrongPassages: His associative essay never linked one image or idea to another.
The sealed cube was redesigned to be associative: no doors between rooms.
She preferred associative notes that listed facts in isolation with no connections.

memoryTip: In-e-luctable: you can’t struggle free — the outcome is locked in.
correctPassage: Climate models point to ineluctable warming under current emissions paths.
wrongPassages: He called the puzzle ineluctable after solving it in under a minute.
Voters tabled the ineluctable transit tax that most riders already supported.
The coach treated the loss as ineluctable, then changed strategy and won the rematch.

memoryTip: Thin as a tenuous thread — a weak link that may snap.
correctPassage: The link between the two studies remains tenuous at best.
wrongPassages: Their tenuous alliance has held firm through three decades of crisis.
She built a tenuous case packed with undisputed documents and witnesses.
The bridge’s tenuous steel beams made engineers confident it would last a century.

definition: to fail by trying to do or control too much
memoryTip: Reach too far — stretch beyond your power and fall short.
correctPassage: Critics accused the agency of regulatory overreach into local decisions.
wrongPassages: The careful plan showed overreach by staying well within the budget.
Her modest goals were praised as overreach by colleagues who wanted more ambition.
With limited staff, their overreach kept projects small and fully finished.
